title: John the Evangelist (27 December)
hookLine: the beloved disciple, the eagle, and the one the fourth Gospel places at the cross

cards: "Lord, who is it?" A question asked at supper on the night before the cross. Jesus has just said that one of the twelve will betray him.
Peter wants a name, so he signals to the disciple closest to Jesus, the one leaning against his chest. That disciple leans back and asks. The Gospel gives him no name there, only a description.
Today, two days after Christmas, the Church keeps the feast of the man tradition says that description belongs to.

teach.b: Here's the description, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now there was leaning on Jesus' bosom one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved."

John's Gospel comes back to it more than once, the disciple whom Jesus loved, and never gives his name. The Church's tradition identifies him with John the apostle, son of Zebedee, and names the fourth Gospel after him.
Some modern readers wonder whether he was someone else.

teach.h: A DISCIPLE NAMED ONLY BY LOVE.
teach.b: The text leaves him unnamed, and that silence may be the point: a disciple known only by being loved. Then the cross.
He stands beside the mother of Jesus, and Jesus says to her, "Woman, behold thy son." And to him, "Behold thy mother." From that hour, the Gospel says, he took her into his own home.
Catholic tradition reads that as Mary given to every disciple, not only one. On Easter morning he runs to the empty tomb with Peter and gets there first.
And at the very end, the Gospel says this is the disciple who bears witness to these things and wrote them down. In Christian art he often has an eagle.

Tradition gives each Gospel writer a living creature from the visions of Ezekiel and the Apocalypse, and John gets the eagle, because, the old explanation goes, his Gospel flies high from its first line: In the beginning was the Word.

teach.h: THE EAGLE AND THE RESTING HEAD.
teach.b: So one man carries two pictures: the eagle soaring, and the head resting on a friend's chest.
This week brought Nicholas giving in secret, Juan Diego the littlest son, the holy house of Loreto, Lucy's light, Kanty's coat, and our first parents. It ends here, at the supper table.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Saint John, apostle and evangelist, on 27 December, inside the Christmas octave; in some places wine is blessed on his day, a custom tied to a story people tell about him.

games.q: you're the beloved disciple at supper. Jesus has just said one of you will betray him, and Peter is beckoning to you. what do you do?
o: lean back and quietly ask Jesus who it is
stand up and demand a name for everyone
games.why: he leans back against Jesus and asks who it is. closeness, not a speech, is how the Gospel shows him.

practice: Lean back against something that can hold you, a high-backed chair, a wall, a pillow, and let your head rest instead of holding itself up. Remember the beloved disciple at that table, close enough to ask a quiet question.
If you pray, rest there with Jesus without asking for anything at all; if you don't, simply let the chair and the quiet hold you.

wordCard.voice: Evangelist. The disciple whom Jesus loved, as tradition identifies him: at the supper, at the cross, at the tomb, and marked in art by the eagle. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek of John 13:23: whom Jesus loved. the phrase the Gospel uses instead of a name.

carryVoice: Your line: the beloved disciple. The Gospel gives him no other name. Go gently.
